newsitem.title: NAMIBIA: Good rains in Namibia could ease long drought.
newsitem.headline: Good rains in Namibia could ease long drought.

text.p: First good rains in some parts of Namibia have raised hopes among farmers of an end to the country's decade-long drought.

The water level of the Hardap Dam, the country's biggest reservoir about 250km (156 miles) south of the capital Windhoek, rose to 80 percent from a 12 percent low as rain fell over southern, central and eastern parts, figures from the water affairs department showed.
Namibia usually receives between 600 and 700mm of rain annually, but figures show that 80mm has already fallen in the east since the start of the rainfall season in October.
Namibia Agricultural Union executive manager Gert Grobler said commercial farmers had been able to plant various crops including maize, groundnuts, cotton and sunflowers.
Cattle farmers also hoped to rebuild their reduced stocks with improved pastures.
"We believe that the pasture will recover even if it won't be as good as it should be," Grobler told Reuters.
He said agricultural output, dominated by beef sales, would be down this year mainly because it had been pushed up in 1996 by emergency livestock slaughter.
Grobler said farmers would face cash-flow shortages as they tried to rebuild their stocks from current core herds.
The Agricultural Bank of Namibia is, however, still cautious about a recovery in the cattle sector and said it was not yet considering offering hard-up farmers special credit facilities.

"We are not offering any special credit facilities at this stage because a lot of grass has dried out and the reports we have received is that regrowth (of pastures) is very slow," a senior bank official told Reuters.

Kaj Hansen of the Namibia Early Warning and Food Information System said crops had been planted late in the north and northwest, especially around the Kavango and Ovambo regions, which had not seen good rains.
He said if current long-term forecasts of a "normal" rainfall season proved correct, there was still time to produce good crops especially the fast-growing varieties.
Johan Beyers of the Namibian Weather Bureau said the recent rains were not unusual.

"It's just a fact that because of the last few years of dry weather we're not used to rain anymore so we take this rainfall as something abnormal. If you look back rainfall like this is not exceptional."
Beyers added that just getting back to normal would be a big improvement after years of drought.
